paragraphs.modern: 'In the magnificent speech you have just given, my dear Agathon, I think you were right to propose speaking first of the nature of Love and afterwards of his works — that is a way of beginning I very much approve of. And since you have spoken so eloquently of his nature, may I ask you something further: is love the love of something, or of nothing? Here I must explain myself. I do not want you to say that Love is the love of a father or of a mother, as if I were asking whose child he is — that would be ridiculous. Rather, I want you to answer as you would if I asked whether a father is a father of something. You would have no difficulty in replying that he is the father of a son or a daughter, and that answer would be right.'
paragraphs.notes: Opening and closing single quotes added: the current text had none, although this is Socrates' speech after 'Socrates then proceeded as follows' (6.12) and the replies in 7.1-7.9 are single-quoted. Per the fix goal, 'as if I were asking whose child he is' makes clear that the ridiculous question ruled out is Love's parentage; Jowett's 'the love of a father or of a mother' wording is kept. The two fragments become full sentences, and the father-of-a-son-or-daughter analogy is kept.

paragraphs.modern: 'Keep in mind what love is love of, and tell me what I want to know: does Love desire the very thing he is love of?'
paragraphs.notes: 'He' for Love, matching the KEEP line 7.12 ('does he possess').

paragraphs.modern: 'No,' replied Socrates, 'I'd like you to consider whether "necessarily," and not "probably," is the right word. The inference that he who desires something lacks something, and that he who desires nothing lacks nothing, is in my judgment, Agathon, absolutely and necessarily true. What do you think?'
paragraphs.notes: The quotation marks around 'necessarily' are restored, as double quotes because they fall inside single-quoted speech, and the word is set against Agathon's 'probably' from 7.13. 'In want of' becomes 'lacks', following the glossary.

paragraphs.modern: 'And yet,' added Socrates, 'suppose a man who is strong desires to be strong, or a man who is swift desires to be swift, or a man who is healthy desires to be healthy. In that case he might be thought to desire something he already has, or already is. I give this example so that we do not fall into a misunderstanding. For we must suppose, Agathon, that people who possess these qualities have their advantages at the present moment, whether they like it or not; and who can desire what he already has? So when someone says, "I am well and wish to be well," or "I am rich and wish to be rich, and I desire simply to have what I have," we shall reply to him: "My friend, you have wealth and health and strength, and what you want is to go on having them; for at this moment, whether you like it or not, you have them. So when you say that you desire what you have and nothing else, don't you really mean that you want to have in the future what you have now?" He must agree with us — mustn't he?'
paragraphs.notes: Rendered as indirect speech, 'when you say that you desire what you have and nothing else', to avoid a third level of quotation marks. The question keeps 'must' so that Agathon's KEEP reply 'He must' (7.21) still fits.

paragraphs.modern: 'Then he, and everyone else who desires, desires what he does not already have, what lies in the future and not in the present, what he does not possess, what he is not, and what he lacks. So these are the kinds of things that love and desire seek?'
paragraphs.notes: All five of Jowett's items are kept in order, including his repeated 'which he has not', rendered 'what he does not possess'.

paragraphs.modern: 'Now then,' said Socrates, 'let us sum up the argument. First, is love not the love of something — and of something, too, that a man lacks?'
paragraphs.notes: 'A man lacks' echoes the KEEP recap in 7.32 ('something which a man wants and has not').

paragraphs.modern: 'Remember, too, what you said in your speech — or if you do not remember, I will remind you. You said that the love of the beautiful set the realm of the gods in order, because there is no love of ugly things. Didn't you say something like that?'
paragraphs.notes: This matches R3's repaired 6.4 ('Love set the realm of the gods in order ... Love has nothing to do with ugliness'), which Socrates is quoting here.

paragraphs.modern: 'Yes, my friend, and the remark was a just one. And if this is true, Love is the love of beauty and not of ugliness?'
'You made a very good speech, Agathon,' replied Socrates, 'but there is still one small question I would like to ask: isn't the good also the beautiful?'
'Then in lacking the beautiful, love also lacks the good?'
paragraphs.notes: 'Lacking/lacks' follows the glossary, so the step reads as a lack and not a desire.

paragraphs.modern: 'No, beloved Agathon — it is the truth that you cannot refute, for Socrates is easily refuted.
paragraphs.notes: There is deliberately no closing quote. Socrates' speech runs on without a break into 7.45 and continues to 7.68, so under the glossary's multi-paragraph rule the quote closes only where the speech ends (R3 did the same across 6.9-6.10).

paragraphs.modern: 'And now I will leave you in peace, and tell a story about love that I heard from Diotima of Mantineia, a woman wise in this and in many other kinds of knowledge. Long ago, when the Athenians offered sacrifices before the plague came, she delayed the disease for ten years. She was my teacher in the art of love, and I shall repeat to you what she said to me. I will begin with the points Agathon admitted, which are nearly, if not quite, the same as those I admitted to the wise woman when she questioned me. I think this will be the easiest way, and I shall take both parts myself, hers and mine, as well as I can. As you suggested, Agathon, I must speak first of the being and nature of Love, and then of his works. First I said to her in nearly the same words that Agathon used to me: that Love was a mighty god, and beautiful as well. And she proved to me, just as I proved to him, that by my own argument Love was neither beautiful nor good. "What do you mean, Diotima?" I said. "Is love then bad and ugly?" "Hush," she cried. "Must whatever is not beautiful be ugly?" "Certainly," I said. "And is whatever is not wise ignorant? Don't you see that there is something in between wisdom and ignorance?" "And what might that be?" I said.
paragraphs.notes: Jowett's notes '(compare 1 Alcibiades)', '(compare Gorgias)' and '(supra)' are omitted, as before. Fair/foul become beautiful/ugly, so the recap visibly repeats the argument with Agathon. 'Evil' becomes 'bad' as the opposite of 'good', here and in 7.46 and 7.52. Quote convention for 7.45-7.68: Socrates' speech to the company is in single quotes and reopens at the start of every paragraph; the Diotima dialogue inside it is in double quotes; a quotation inside Diotima's speech takes single quotes (7.50, 7.51, 7.56). The speech is not closed here because it continues into 7.46.

paragraphs.modern: '"Right opinion," she replied. "As you know, right opinion means being right without being able to give a reason for it. So it is not knowledge, for how can there be knowledge without reason? Nor is it ignorance, for ignorance can never arrive at the truth. Clearly, then, it is something in between ignorance and wisdom." "Quite true," I replied. "Then do not insist," she said, "that whatever is not beautiful must be ugly, or that whatever is not good must be bad. And do not conclude that because love is not beautiful and good, he must therefore be ugly and bad; for he is in between them." "Well," I said, "surely Love is admitted by everyone to be a great god." "By those who know, or by those who do not know?" "By everyone." "And how, Socrates," she said with a smile, "can Love be admitted to be a great god by those who say that he is not a god at all?" "And who are they?" I said. "You and I are two of them," she replied. "How can that be?" I said. "It is easy to see," she replied, "for you yourself would admit that the gods are happy and beautiful — of course you would. Would you dare to say that any god was not?" "Certainly not," I replied. "And by the happy, you mean those who possess good or beautiful things?" "Yes." "And you admitted that Love, because he lacks good and beautiful things, desires the very things he lacks?" "Yes, I did." "But how can he be a god if he has no share in what is good or beautiful?" "Impossible." "Then you see that you too deny that Love is a god."
paragraphs.notes: Right opinion is explained in plain sentences, with Jowett's two reasons (it cannot give a reason, so it is not knowledge; it reaches the truth, so it is not ignorance). Every step of the argument that Socrates too denies Love is a god is kept.

paragraphs.modern: '"What then is Love?" I asked. "Is he mortal?" "No." "What then?" "As in the earlier case, he is neither mortal nor immortal, but in between the two." "What is he, Diotima?" "He is a great spirit (daimon), and like all spirits he is midway between the divine and the mortal." "And what," I said, "is his power?" "He interprets," she replied, "between gods and men. He carries the prayers and sacrifices of men across to the gods, and brings the commands and replies of the gods to men. He is the mediator who spans the gulf that divides them, and so in him everything is bound together. Through him the arts of the prophet and the priest find their way, with their sacrifices and mysteries and charms, and all prophecy and incantation. For God does not mix with man; all communication and conversation between God and man, whether man is awake or asleep, is carried on through Love. The wisdom which understands this is spiritual; all other wisdom, such as that of the arts and crafts, is lowly and workaday. Now these spirits, or in-between powers, are many and of many kinds, and one of them is Love." "And who," I said, "was his father, and who was his mother?" "The story," she said, "will take time; but I will tell you all the same. On Aphrodite's birthday the gods held a feast, and one of the guests was the god Poros, or Plenty, who is the son of Metis, or Discretion — that is, cunning intelligence. When the feast was over, Penia, or Poverty, came to the door to beg, as beggars do at a feast.
paragraphs.notes: '(daimon)' is kept. 'Intercourse and converse' becomes 'communication and conversation', and 'mean and vulgar' becomes 'lowly and workaday'. Jowett's 'Discretion' is kept with a gloss ('cunning intelligence'), because the word now suggests tact. Diotima's speech runs on into 7.48, so neither quote is closed.

paragraphs.modern: '"Now Plenty, who was drunk on nectar (there was no wine in those days), went into the garden of Zeus and fell into a heavy sleep. And Poverty, thinking of her own hard circumstances, plotted to have a child by him; so she lay down at his side and conceived Love. Love is Aphrodite's follower and attendant, partly because he is by nature a lover of the beautiful, and because Aphrodite is herself beautiful, and also because he was born on her birthday. His fortunes match his parentage. In the first place, he is always poor, and far from being tender and beautiful, as most people imagine him. He is rough and dirty, with no shoes and no house to live in. He sleeps on the bare ground, exposed under the open sky, in the streets or in doorways; and like his mother he is always in need. But he also partly resembles his father, and like him he is always scheming to win the beautiful and the good. He is bold, enterprising and strong, a mighty hunter, always weaving some intrigue or other, keen in the pursuit of wisdom, full of resources; a philosopher at all times, and formidable as an enchanter, a sorcerer and a sophist, one of those clever professional arguers. By nature he is neither mortal nor immortal: at one moment, when he has plenty, he is alive and flourishing; at another he is dead; and then he comes alive again, because of his father's nature.
paragraphs.notes: The paragraph opens with both quote levels, because Socrates' speech and Diotima's story both continue from 7.47. The three reasons Love follows Aphrodite get a sentence of their own. 'Plotting against' becomes 'scheming to win', 'terrible' becomes 'formidable', and the sophist gloss is in line with R1's 'professional teachers' at 1.46. 'Always in distress' becomes 'always in need', its older sense. Every trait is kept in order.

paragraphs.modern: '"But whatever flows in to him is always flowing out again, and so he is never in need and never rich; and he is also in between ignorance and knowledge. The truth of the matter is this: no god is a philosopher, a seeker after wisdom, for he is wise already; nor does any man who is wise seek after wisdom. Neither do the ignorant seek after wisdom. For this is what is bad about ignorance: someone who is neither good nor wise is nevertheless satisfied with himself, and he has no desire for what he does not feel he lacks." "But who, then, Diotima," I said, "are the lovers of wisdom, if they are neither the wise nor the foolish?" "A child could answer that question," she replied. "They are those who are in between the two, and Love is one of them. For wisdom is one of the most beautiful things, and Love is love of the beautiful; and so Love is also a philosopher, a lover of wisdom, and as a lover of wisdom he is in between the wise and the ignorant. His birth explains this too, for his father is rich and wise, and his mother poor and foolish. Such, my dear Socrates, is the nature of the spirit Love. Your mistaken idea of him was very natural. From what you say, I imagine it came from confusing love with the beloved — what loves with what is loved — and that made you think that love was entirely beautiful. For it is the beloved who is truly beautiful, and delicate, and perfect, and blessed; but what loves has a different nature, the one I have described."
paragraphs.notes: 'What loves with what is loved' makes the confusion explicit without adding a claim; the description of what loves is left to what Diotima has just said. The current text had no opening quote here; both levels are now reopened.

paragraphs.modern: 'I said, "Well said, my friend from Mantineia. But if Love is as you say, what use is he to men?" "That, Socrates," she replied, "I will try to explain. I have already spoken of his nature and his birth, and you agree that love is love of the beautiful. But someone may ask: what is it about the beautiful that love wants, Socrates and Diotima? Or rather, let me put the question more clearly: when a man loves the beautiful, what does he desire?" I answered her, "That the beautiful may be his." "Still," she said, "that answer raises a further question: what does possessing beauty give him?" "To what you have asked," I replied, "I have no answer ready." "Then," she said, "let me put the word 'good' in place of the beautiful, and ask the question once more: if the one who loves loves the good, what is it that he loves?" "The possession of the good," I said. "And what does someone who possesses the good gain?" "Happiness," I replied. "That question is easier to answer." "Yes," she said, "the happy are made happy by acquiring good things. And there is no need to ask why a man desires happiness; that answer is already final." "You are right," I said.
paragraphs.notes: The current text had its opening quote after 'I said,'; Socrates' single quote now opens the paragraph. 'O thou stranger woman' becomes 'my friend from Mantineia': 'from Mantineia' keeps her status as a visitor from abroad, and 'my friend' is Socrates' polite address elsewhere ('Yes, my friend', 7.30). Both 'stranger' and a bare 'lady' would mislead or sound brusque today. The imagined question is left without inner quote marks, as in Jowett, and its wording is made plain. 'Good' is in single quotes as a third-level quotation, inside Diotima's double-quoted speech inside Socrates' single-quoted speech.

paragraphs.modern: '"And is this wish, this desire, common to all? Do all men always desire their own good, or only some men? What do you say?" "All men," I replied. "The desire is common to all." "Why, then, Socrates," she asked, "do we not say that all men love, but only some of them? Yet you say that all men are always loving the same things." "I wonder about that myself," I said. "There is nothing to wonder at," she replied. "The reason is that one part of love is separated off and given the name of the whole, while the other parts have other names." "Give me an example," I said. She answered me as follows: "Take poetry, which, as you know, is complex and takes many forms. Our word for poetry literally means 'making': every act of creation, every passage from not-being into being, is poetry, or making. The processes of all the arts are creative, and so the masters of all the arts are poets, or makers." "Very true." "Still," she said, "you know that they are not called poets, but have other names. Only one part of the art, which is separated off from the rest and is concerned with music and meter, is called poetry; and only those who have poetry in this sense of the word are called poets." "Very true," I said. "And the same holds for love.
paragraphs.notes: 'Our word for poetry literally means making' gives the Greek sense in Diotima's own voice, so the reader sees that every maker is strictly a 'poet' although the name is kept for verse-makers. The 'whereas' fragment becomes 'Yet you say ...'. Diotima's speech continues into 7.52, so neither quote is closed.

paragraphs.modern: '"For you may say, in general, that every desire for good things and for happiness is simply the great and subtle power of love. But those who are drawn to him by some other path, whether the path of making money, or athletics, or philosophy, are not called lovers. Only those whose love takes one particular form are given the name that belongs to the whole: they alone are said to love, or to be lovers." "You are probably right," I replied. "Yes," she added, "and you hear people say that lovers are seeking their other half. But I say that they are seeking neither the half of themselves nor the whole, unless that half or whole is also something good. And men will cut off their own hands and feet and throw them away, if they are bad. For people do not love what is their own just because it is their own — unless perhaps someone calls whatever belongs to him good, and whatever belongs to another bad. For there is nothing that men love but the good. Is there anything else?" "Certainly not, I should say." "Then," she said, "the simple truth is that men love the good." "Yes," I said. "And to this we must add that they love the possession of the good?" "Yes, that must be added." "And not only the possession, but the everlasting possession of the good?" "That must be added too." "Then love," she said, "may be described in general as the love of the everlasting possession of the good?" "That is most true."
paragraphs.notes: 'I dare say that you are right' becomes 'You are probably right'. The 'other half' allusion is kept without naming Aristophanes, which would be anachronistic in Diotima's mouth. 'The everlasting possession of the good' is kept word for word, because 7.54 and 7.55 recall it.

paragraphs.modern: '"Then if this is the nature of love," she said, "can you tell me further how it is pursued? What are they doing, those who show all this eagerness and heat that is called love? And what is the goal they have in view? Answer me." "No, Diotima," I replied. "If I had known, I would not have marveled at your wisdom, or come to learn from you about this very thing." "Well," she said, "I will teach you. The goal they have in view is birth in beauty, whether of body or of soul." "I do not understand you," I said. "The oracle needs explaining." "I will make my meaning clearer," she replied. "I mean that all human beings are pregnant, in body and in soul. At a certain age human nature desires to procreate — and procreation must take place in beauty, not in ugliness. This procreation is the union of man and woman, and it is a divine thing; for conception and reproduction are something immortal in a mortal creature, and they can never happen in what is out of harmony with the divine. But the ugly is always out of harmony with the divine, and the beautiful is in harmony with it.
paragraphs.notes: 'Birth in beauty' is kept as Diotima's riddle. 'Procreation' is kept, since it is current English, and 'generation' becomes 'reproduction'. The inharmonious step is spelled out with the fix goal's wording, which repeats 'the divine'.

paragraphs.modern: '"Beauty, then, is the Fate and the goddess of childbirth who presides over birth. So when a pregnant creature comes near beauty, it becomes gracious; it relaxes and opens; it is kindly, and it gives birth and bears fruit. But at the sight of ugliness it frowns and contracts and feels pain; it turns away and shrivels up, and, not without a pang, holds back from giving birth. That is why, when the time comes and the pregnant creature is full to bursting, there is such a flutter and ecstasy about beauty, because the approach of beauty relieves the pains of labor. For love, Socrates, is not, as you imagine, love of the beautiful only." "What then?" "The love of reproduction and of birth in beauty." "Yes," I said. "Yes, indeed," she replied. "But why of reproduction?" "Because for a mortal creature, reproduction is a kind of eternity and immortality," she replied. "And if, as we have already agreed, love is of the everlasting possession of the good, then all men must necessarily desire immortality together with the good. So love is also of immortality."
paragraphs.notes: The fix goal asks for plain childbirth language. So Jowett's 'refrains from conception' becomes 'holds back from giving birth', and 'the hour of conception' becomes 'when the time comes'. Propitious, diffusive and benign become gracious, relaxes and opens, kindly. 'Travail' becomes 'labor'. As in Jowett, the speaker of 'But why of reproduction?' is left unassigned.

paragraphs.modern: 'All this she taught me at various times when she spoke about love. And I remember her once saying to me, "What is the cause, Socrates, of love and of the desire that goes with it? Don't you see how all animals, birds as well as beasts, are in agony when they catch the infection of love in their desire to reproduce? It begins with the desire to mate; then comes care for their young, for whose sake the weakest are ready to fight the strongest to the death, and to die for them, and will let themselves be tormented by hunger or suffer anything else in order to provide for their young. Man, one may suppose, acts like this from reason; but why should animals have these passionate feelings? Can you tell me why?" Again I replied that I did not know. She said to me, "And do you expect ever to become a master in the art of love, if you do not know this?" "But I have told you already, Diotima, that my ignorance is the reason I come to you; for I know that I need a teacher. So tell me the cause of this, and of the other mysteries of love." "If you believe that love is of the immortal, as we have agreed several times," she said, "then do not be surprised. For here again, and on the same principle, mortal nature is seeking, as far as it can, to be everlasting and immortal; and it can achieve this only by reproduction, because reproduction always leaves behind a new existence in place of the old.
paragraphs.notes: 'Marvel not ... if you believe' becomes a conditional ('If you believe ... then do not be surprised'). 'I want a teacher' becomes 'I need a teacher', since 'want' here means lack. 'The desire of union' becomes 'the desire to mate'. Diotima's speech continues into 7.56.

paragraphs.modern: '"Indeed, even in the life of a single individual there is succession, not complete sameness. A man is called the same person; and yet in the short time between youth and old age, the time in which every living creature is said to be alive and to remain the same, he is going through a constant process of loss and renewal: his hair, flesh, bones, blood and whole body are always changing. And this is true not only of the body but also of the soul. Our habits, tempers, opinions, desires, pleasures, pains and fears never stay the same in any of us, but are always coming and going. It is equally true of knowledge; and, what is still more surprising to us mortals, not only do whole branches of knowledge spring up and decay in us, so that we are never the same with respect to them, but each one of them, individually, undergoes the same change. For what does the word 'recollection' imply, if not that knowledge departs? Knowledge is always being forgotten, and it is renewed and preserved by recollection, so that it seems to be the same although in reality it is new. That is the law of succession by which all mortal things are preserved: not by remaining exactly the same, but by replacement, the old and worn-out mortal thing leaving behind another that is new and similar. The divine is different; it is always the same and never another. In this way, Socrates, the mortal body, or anything else mortal, shares in immortality; but the immortal shares in it in another way.
paragraphs.notes: Jowett's one long 'recollection' question becomes four sentences. His closing '-- unlike the divine ...' becomes its own sentence. 'Recollection' takes single quotes as a third-level quotation. 'Sciences' becomes 'branches of knowledge'. 'The immortal in another way' is completed as 'shares in it in another way'.

paragraphs.modern: '"So do not be surprised at the love that all men have for their children; for that universal love and concern is for the sake of immortality."
paragraphs.notes: 'Do not be surprised' matches 7.55. Diotima's speech closes here, but Socrates' continues into 7.58.

paragraphs.modern: 'I was astonished at her words, and said, "Is this really true, wise Diotima?" And she answered with all the authority of an accomplished sophist, one of those professional teachers of wisdom: "Of that, Socrates, you may be sure. Just think of the ambition of men, and you will be amazed at how senseless their ways are, unless you consider how they are stirred by the love of an immortal fame. They are ready to run all kinds of risks, far greater than they would have run for their children, and to spend money, and undergo any sort of toil, and even to die, for the sake of leaving behind them a name that will be eternal. Do you imagine that Alcestis would have died to save Admetus, or Achilles to avenge Patroclus, or your own Codrus, the early king of Athens, to preserve the kingdom for his sons, if they had not imagined that the memory of their virtues, which still lives on among us, would be immortal? Indeed," she said, "I am convinced that all men do all things, and the better they are the more they do them, in the hope of the glorious fame of immortal virtue; for they desire the immortal.
paragraphs.notes: The sophist gloss ('professional teachers') matches R1 at 1.46; Socrates' irony is left in the phrase itself. Codrus is identified in three words, and Alcestis and Achilles are left as they are. Diotima's speech continues into 7.59, as in Jowett, who opens a new quotation there without closing this one.

paragraphs.modern: '"Those who are pregnant in body only turn to women and have children — this is the form their love takes. Their children, they hope, will preserve their memory and give them the blessedness and immortality that they desire in the future. But souls that are pregnant — for there certainly are men who are more creative in their souls than in their bodies — conceive what it is proper for the soul to conceive or contain. And what are these conceptions? Wisdom and virtue in general. And such creators are the poets, and all the artists who deserve the name of inventor. But by far the greatest and most beautiful kind of wisdom is the one concerned with the ordering of states and families, which is called self-control and justice. And when a man has had the seed of these planted in him from his youth, and is himself inspired, then when he comes to maturity he wants to beget offspring and bring them to birth.
paragraphs.notes: 'Temperance' becomes 'self-control', following the glossary. Jowett's 'giving them' is a slip for 'give them' and is read that way, as in the current text.

paragraphs.modern: '"He wanders about seeking beauty so that he may beget offspring — for in ugliness he will beget nothing — and so he naturally embraces beautiful bodies rather than ugly ones. Above all, when he finds a soul that is beautiful and noble and well brought up, he embraces the two, body and soul, in one person. To such a person he talks freely about virtue, and about what a good man is and how he should live; and he tries to educate him. And through contact with the beautiful one, who is always present in his memory even when absent, he gives birth to what he conceived long ago, and together with him he nurtures what he has brought forth. And so the two of them are married by a far closer bond, and share a closer friendship, than those who have mortal children together, for the children they have in common are more beautiful and more immortal. Who, when he thinks of Homer and Hesiod and the other great poets, would not rather have their children than ordinary human ones? Who would not want to rival them in creating children like theirs, which have preserved their memory and given them everlasting glory? Or who would not want such children as the lawgiver Lycurgus left behind him in his laws, to be the saviors not only of Lacedaemon, that is, Sparta, but of Hellas, the whole of Greece, as one might say?
paragraphs.notes: 'Body and soul' makes clear what 'the two' are. 'The beautiful one' is read as the person the lover is educating, whom he nurtures his offspring 'together with'. Jowett's 'married' image is kept. The Lycurgus, Lacedaemon and Hellas glosses are in line with R3's 'the Lacedaemonians, the Spartans' at 5.5.

paragraphs.modern: '"There is Solon, too, the revered father of Athenian law; and there are many others in many other places, both among Hellenes and among barbarians — Greeks and non-Greeks alike — who have given the world many noble works and have been the parents of every kind of virtue. Many temples have been raised in their honor for the sake of children such as theirs; but no temple was ever raised in anyone's honor for the sake of his mortal children.
paragraphs.notes: The words 'Hellenes' and 'barbarians' are kept, and 'Greeks and non-Greeks alike' shows that 'barbarians' just means foreigners.

paragraphs.modern: '"These are the lesser mysteries of love, the first rites of initiation, into which even you, Socrates, may enter. Then there are the greater and more hidden mysteries, the final rites, which are the crown of these; and the lesser mysteries, if you pursue them in the right spirit, will lead you to them. Whether you will be able to attain to those, I do not know. But I will do my utmost to teach you, and you must follow if you can. For whoever would go about this matter rightly should begin in youth by turning to beautiful bodies. First, if his guide leads him rightly, he should love one such body only, and out of that love he should create beautiful thoughts. Soon he will see for himself that the beauty of one body is akin to the beauty of another. And then, if beauty of body in general is what he pursues, how foolish he would be not to recognize that the beauty in every body is one and the same! When he sees this, he will relax his intense passion for the one, looking down on it and thinking it a small thing, and he will become a lover of all beautiful bodies. In the next stage he will consider the beauty of the mind more precious than outward, bodily beauty.
paragraphs.notes: 'First rites of initiation' and 'final rites' show the mysteries as stages of a religious initiation. 'Forms' becomes 'bodies', following the glossary. The Gutenberg typo 'is and the same' is read as 'one and the same', as in the current text. 'Abate' becomes 'relax', not 'let go of', so that it stays true to 'abate' (lessen).

paragraphs.modern: '"So even if someone with a virtuous soul has only a little physical beauty, he will be content to love him and care for him, and will seek out and give birth to thoughts that may make the young better, until he is compelled to contemplate and see the beauty of institutions and laws, and to understand that the beauty of them all is of one family, and that bodily beauty is a small thing. After laws and institutions he will go on to the branches of knowledge, so that he may see their beauty. He will not be like a servant in love with the beauty of one young man, or one man, or one institution, himself a slave, petty and narrow-minded. Instead, turning toward the vast sea of beauty and contemplating it, he will create many beautiful and noble thoughts and notions in a boundless love of wisdom, until, growing and gaining strength on that shore, he is at last granted the vision of a single kind of knowledge, the knowledge of beauty everywhere. I will now go on to this; please give me your very best attention:
paragraphs.notes: The soul/him pronoun shift is fixed with 'someone with a virtuous soul ... love him'. The servant-and-sea contrast is split into two sentences. The colon at the end is kept from Jowett, because it leads into 7.64.

paragraphs.modern: '"Whoever has been instructed this far in the things of love, and has learned to see beautiful things in their proper order and succession, will, as he comes toward the end, suddenly perceive something wondrously beautiful in its nature — and this, Socrates, is the goal of all our earlier efforts. In the first place, it is everlasting: it does not grow and decay, or wax and wane. Secondly, it is not beautiful from one point of view and ugly from another; not beautiful at one time, or in one relation, or in one place, and ugly at another time, or in another relation, or in another place, as if it were beautiful to some and ugly to others. Nor does it take the likeness of a face or hands or any other part of the body; nor does it take the form of any speech or knowledge; nor does it exist in any other being, such as an animal, or the heavens, or the earth, or any other place. It is beauty absolute, separate, simple and everlasting, which, without growing less or greater, or changing in any way, is imparted to the ever-growing and perishing beauties of all other things. When someone rises from these under the influence of true love and begins to perceive that beauty, he is not far from the end.
paragraphs.notes: The cumulative list is kept, and 'nor' is repeated so that each item says what this beauty is not. The last sentence is un-inverted so that 'that beauty' cannot be read as the start of a that-clause.

paragraphs.modern: '"And the true order of going, or of being led by another, to the things of love is this: to begin from the beauties of earth and climb upward for the sake of that other beauty, using these only as steps — from one beautiful body to two, and from two to all beautiful bodies; from beautiful bodies to beautiful practices, and from beautiful practices to beautiful notions; until from beautiful notions he arrives at the notion of absolute beauty, and at last knows what the essence of beauty is. This, my dear Socrates," said the woman from Mantineia, "is the life above all others that a man should live, in the contemplation of absolute beauty. If you once saw that beauty, you would see that it is not to be measured against gold, and clothes, and beautiful boys and young men, whose presence now entrances you. You and many others would be content to live just seeing them and talking with them, without food or drink, if that were possible — you want only to look at them and to be with them. But what if a man had eyes to see the true beauty — the divine beauty, I mean, pure and clear and unmixed, not clogged with the pollutions of mortality and all the colors and vanities of human life? What if he could look there, and hold communion with that true beauty, simple and divine?
paragraphs.notes: Every rung of the ladder is kept in order: one body, two, all beautiful bodies, practices, notions, then absolute beauty. 'The stranger of Mantineia' becomes 'the woman from Mantineia', keeping Jowett's spelling of the place name. 'Holding converse with' becomes 'hold communion with', which leads into 'that communion' in 7.66.

paragraphs.modern: '"Remember that only there, in that communion, as he beholds beauty with the eye of the mind, will he be able to give birth not to images of beauty but to realities, because what he has hold of is not an image but a reality. And by giving birth to true virtue and nurturing it, he can become the friend of God and be immortal, if any mortal man can. Would that be a life to despise?"
paragraphs.notes: Diotima's speech ends here. Socrates' speech continues into 7.67 and 7.68, so the single quote is not closed; the current text had closed it here and reopened it at 7.67.

paragraphs.modern: 'Such, Phaedrus — and I speak not only to you, but to all of you — were the words of Diotima; and I am persuaded that they are true. And being persuaded, I try to persuade others too that, in reaching this goal, human nature will not easily find a better helper than Love. And so I say that every man ought to honor him, as I myself honor him. I walk in his ways, and I urge others to do the same; and now and always I praise the power and spirit of Love as well as I am able.
paragraphs.notes: What every man ought to do is now separate from what Socrates himself does, so 'my ability' no longer attaches to 'every man'. Love is capitalized here, as the god honored and followed ('walk in his ways').

paragraphs.modern: 'What I have said, Phaedrus, you may call a speech in praise of Love, or anything else you please.'
paragraphs.notes: 'Encomium' becomes 'a speech in praise of Love', matching R3's 5.16 and 'the praise of Love' in 1.47. Socrates' ironic 'or anything else you please' is kept. The single quote that has been open since 7.44 closes here.
